nameStory: Dotted duckweed gets its name from the tiny dark dots or spots that pepper its small floating leaves, making it look like someone sprinkled pepper on regular duckweed. The 'duckweed' part of the name comes from how waterfowl love to munch on these tiny floating plants, which carpet the surface of quiet waters like a green blanket.
description: Dotted duckweed is one of the world's smallest flowering plants, forming tiny floating mats on the surface of still waters. Each individual plant is just a small, oval-shaped leaf (called a frond) about the size of a pinky nail, with short roots dangling underneath. These little green discs multiply rapidly by budding, creating dense carpets that can cover entire ponds or slow-moving streams.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval fronds with distinctive dark spots or dots scattered across the surface, feeling smooth and slightly succulent to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Floats freely on water surface in dense mats, with individual plants connected by thin stems before breaking apart

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Several white, thread-like roots dangle from each frond underwater, typically 1-3 inches long

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual fronds are very small, roughly 2-5mm across, about the size of a match head

habitat: In New England, dotted duckweed is extremely rare, found floating on the surface of quiet, nutrient-rich waters like ponds, slow streams, and ditches. It prefers warm, still waters with plenty of dissolved nutrients and minimal water movement. Look for it in sheltered coves or backwater areas where other duckweeds might also be present.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin active growth as waters warm, budding rapidly to form small colonies floating on the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with dense mats forming quickly in suitable habitat, easily spotted as green carpets on water.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows as temperatures drop, with some plants producing winter buds that sink to the bottom for cold survival.
seasonality.winter: Most visible growth disappears, surviving as dormant buds on pond bottoms until spring warming triggers new growth.

funFact: This tiny plant is actually a world traveler that started in Australia and Southeast Asia but has somehow made its way around the globe, likely hitchhiking on migrating waterfowl's feet and feathers - making each bird an unwitting international plant smuggler!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with common duckweed, but dotted duckweed has those telltale dark spots on its fronds and typically has multiple roots per plant instead of just one. Think 'polka-dot duckweed' - if you see the spots, you've found the rarer species!
contextualKnowledge: Scientists recently moved this species into its own genus (Landoltia) based on DNA studies, so you might see it listed as either Spirodela punctata or Landoltia punctata in different field guides. Both names refer to the same spotted little plant.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Landoltia found in our region, dotted duckweed sits between the smaller Lemna duckweeds (which have single roots) and larger Spirodela duckweeds (which lack the distinctive spotting). Its multiple roots and spotted fronds make it unique among New England's floating aquatic plants.
